headline: Medium prompt-injection and cascading-error risk from AutoGPT filesystem/tool use feeding pdf.js browser-based document processing; no direct data-leak or compliance mismatch is evidenced.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGPT can execute shell and access the filesystem, while pdf.js processes PDF files in browser-based tests. If AutoGPT writes attacker-controlled content into PDFs or adjacent files that pdf.js later opens, instructions can be smuggled through shared files. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so the interaction is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF AutoGPT writes content into a PDF or companion file that pdf.js later opens
IF the two agents share a filesystem without provenance tagging
mitigations: Separate working directories for each agent
Disable automatic opening of files produced by AutoGPT
Add a manual review step before pdf.js processes any AutoGPT output
Use read-only mounts for pdf.js inputs
requires-engineering: add provenance labels to files

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGPT can touch the filesystem and make allowlisted network egress, while pdf.js handles PDF documents but has no network egress. The profiles do not show shared secrets, shared OAuth, or sensitive data classes beyond PDFs, so leakage is limited to a shared-workspace scenario and is not evidenced as default behavior.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace containing sensitive PDFs
IF AutoGPT is configured to read and transmit file contents through its allowlisted egress
mitigations: Use separate workspaces
Restrict AutoGPT egress to non-file endpoints
Store sensitive PDFs outside the shared directory
Review outbound requests from AutoGPT
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGPT can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; pdf.js supports multiple instances and reads PDF files. If both are aimed at the same directory, they can race on shared files or overwrite each other's artifacts. The conflict is plausible from the profiles, though no locking mechanism is documented for the pair.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory
IF AutoGPT generates files that pdf.js also modifies or caches
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Make pdf.js inputs read-only
Serialize writes with a simple operator checklist
Avoid concurrent runs on the same files
requires-engineering: add file locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGPT can generate artifacts from shell/file operations, and pdf.js can consume PDF files in browser-based tests. If pdf.js treats AutoGPT-produced files as authoritative inputs, an error or hallucination in AutoGPT can cascade into downstream rendering or decisions. No verification step is documented in the pair, so the risk is inferred rather than directly observed.
conditions: IF pdf.js consumes AutoGPT output without human verification
IF AutoGPT output is used as the source of truth for a downstream document workflow
mitigations: Require human review before pdf.js ingestion
Compare outputs against original source PDFs
Mark AutoGPT outputs as untrusted by default
Add a checksum check on input files
requires-engineering: implement validation gates

E_compliance.rationale: No compliance mismatch is evidenced. AutoGPT's profile lists no data classes touched or regulated residency constraints, and pdf.js only shows PDF documents with no stated retention, residency, or certification gap. Because the relevant compliance fields are absent, a breach pathway is not established.
conditions: IF either profile later adds regulated data classes such as PHI or EU PII
IF a residency or retention policy mismatch is introduced
mitigations: Document data-class handling before deployment
Confirm retention settings for any regulated PDFs
Review residency requirements if new jurisdictions are added
